summary: Defines general extensions for SDP and the Real Time Streaming Protocol to carry messages from a key management protocol, so media can be secured. It is presented as a framework that one or more key management protocols can use. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a secret video, both sides need to share a key. This adds a place in the call setup messages to carry the key-sharing messages.

questions: secure media key exchange in sdp
what is the sdp key-mgmt attribute
what is the rtsp keymgmt header
subtitle: A way to carry key management messages inside SDP and RTSP so media can be keyed during session setup.

tldr.problem: Secure media such as SRTP needs keys and security parameters, but SDP's single k= field cannot carry the many parameters a key management protocol needs.
tldr.mechanism: A new SDP attribute, key-mgmt, and a new RTSP header, KeyMgmt, carry a protocol identifier plus base64-encoded key management data, and rules explain how to use them with offer/answer, SAP and RTSP.
tldr.outcome: Only the key management protocol's own security protects the keys, so the framework works even when the signaling is not protected end to end. It is useful only together with a key management protocol, and MIKEY is the one it defines.

today: RFC 4567 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the framework and the MIKEY binding described in RFC 3830.

sections.title: Why Put Key Management in the Session Setup
sections.content:
Protecting real-time media with SRTP needs a key management protocol run beforehand. Its job is to establish a security association: one or more keys plus parameters such as cipher and authentication algorithms.

The RFC lists reasons to do this inside session setup. Key data describes how to decrypt the stream just as codec data describes how to decode it. Security for the whole multimedia session can be negotiated at once, and tying keying to the session is easy when the media is already known. It can also save round trips compared with setting security up later, and keys can be negotiated end to end without end-to-end protection of the SDP, which matters when proxies need to read it.

SDP's existing k= field is not enough, because a key management protocol has many more parameters and the field is not extensible. The related approach in SDES (RFC 4568) needs the SDP itself to be protected end to end, whereas this framework protects only the key management parameters and needs no external protection.
sections.plainLanguage: It is easier to agree on the secret code in the same message you use to start the call, instead of making a second call just for that.

sections.title: The key-mgmt Attribute and KeyMgmt Header
sections.content:
Both extensions work the same way: one identifier names the key management protocol (KMPID, letters and digits, case sensitive, lowercase recommended) and one field holds that protocol's data. The data MUST be base64 encoded.

In SDP the attribute is a=key-mgmt:<prtcl-id> <base64 data>. It MAY appear at session level, media level or both, and a media-level attribute overrides a session-level one for that media.

RTSP does not use offer/answer, so a new KeyMgmt header carries the reply. It has a prot parameter and an optional uri parameter naming the session or media context. It is RECOMMENDED in a DESCRIBE response, REQUIRED in SETUP requests, and REQUIRED in a SETUP response when reporting an error. A new RTSP status code, 463, means key management failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has two new boxes: one says which secret-code method is used, and one holds the code message, written in a safe text form.

sections.title: Using It with SDP, SIP and SAP
sections.content:
The key management protocol must be able to finish in at most one request-response exchange. To make an offer, the SDP application puts the protocol id in prtcl-id and the base64-encoded key management message in the data field. The receiver extracts and decodes it and hands it to the key management protocol. If errors occur or the offer is rejected, the session SHALL be aborted unless renegotiation is intended.

With SIP offer/answer, an offerer may list several key management protocols, in order of preference, and the answerer picks one. A failed offer that cannot be renegotiated SHOULD get a 488 Not Acceptable Here. Re-keying is handled as a new offer using the same protocol. If any session-level or media-level attribute fails, the whole session setup is aborted.

With one-way distribution such as SAP, only one protocol SHALL be offered and it must support one-way messages.

To prevent bidding-down attacks, where a man in the middle deletes strong offers so that only a weak one remains, the list of offered protocol identifiers (such as mikey;keyp1;keyp2) MUST be given to each protocol and authenticated by it. Even a single protocol MUST authenticate its own identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: If you offer several secret-code methods, you also sign the list of what you offered, so nobody can quietly cross out the strong ones.

sections.title: Using It with RTSP
sections.content:
For PLAY mode the server SHALL be the initiator. The client sends DESCRIBE, and the server's first key management message arrives in the SDP of the 200 OK. The client replies with a KeyMgmt header in SETUP.

For session-level key management with aggregated control, the reply goes in the first SETUP and its uri is the aggregated control URL. Media later added to the same aggregated session reuses those parameters. For media-level key management, each media stream's SETUP carries its own header. If the server expects key management data in a SETUP and finds none, it SHOULD return 403 Forbidden and abort. If key management fails, it answers with 463.

Re-keying within RTSP is left for further study. Only one key management protocol SHALL be used per session or media level.
sections.plainLanguage: The server shows the code method on the program guide, and the client answers when it asks to start each stream.

sections.title: Adding Protocols and the MIKEY Binding
sections.content:
Not every key management protocol fits. A new one must meet the requirements above, have its identifier registered with IANA, document what it needs from SDP and RTSP, and say how it authenticates the protocol identifier list. The RFC names Kerberos as a possible later user but leaves that to future standardization.

The protocol defined here is MIKEY (RFC 3830), registered with the identifier mikey. MIKEY authenticates the identifier list by carrying it in a General Extension Payload of type SDP IDs, which is integrity protected or signed. The receiver SHALL compare that list with the SDP and SHOULD reject the offer if they differ or verification fails.

For RTSP the server must know the client identity before creating a MIKEY message, so the From header is RECOMMENDED in DESCRIBE. Implementations should expose an interface letting MIKEY learn about the negotiated streams. When mapping SDP media lines to crypto sessions, MIKEY allocates two consecutive Crypto Session numbers per m line.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can invent a new secret-code method, but it has to follow the same rules and be signed up in a public list first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework protects the media session end to end even if setup is secured only hop by hop. If the key management protocol is secure, the SDP can be passed unencrypted without exposing the keys. If SDP is not integrity protected, an active attacker can change attributes undetected, which may indirectly affect the key management or cause denial of service.

The only integrity-protected part of the media description is the set of key management protocols. Injecting an old key management offer into a new SDP is expected to be caught by replay protection. Swapping offers between messages is detected by the reply check or ends up as a denial of service with mismatched keys.

Offering many protocols is only as strong as the weakest one, so an offer MUST NOT contain anything weaker than local policy allows. A declined offer cannot be authenticated, so an attacker could fake errors until the offerer tries a protocol the attacker likes. For that reason, an initiator unsure of the responder's protocols is RECOMMENDED to offer all acceptable ones in a single offer.
sections.plainLanguage: The note itself might be read by others, but the code inside is protected. The worst a trickster can do is stop the call from starting.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR THE SDP ATTRIBUTE AND RTSP HEADER (RFC 4567)

data.title: key-mgmt grammar
data.code:
KMPID = 1*(ALPHA / DIGIT)

key-mgmt-attribute = key-mgmt-att-field ":" key-mgmt-att-value
key-mgmt-att-field = "key-mgmt"
key-mgmt-att-value = 0*1SP prtcl-id SP keymgmt-data
prtcl-id           = KMPID
keymgmt-data       = base64

KeyMgmt = "KeyMgmt" ":" key-mgmt-spec 0*("," key-mgmt-spec)
key-mgmt-spec = "prot" "=" KMPID ";" ["uri" "=" %x22 URI %x22 ";"]

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: A 463 reply would report key management failure.
